conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in this morning for nausea, vomiting, and high blood sugar. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I ate potato salad and meat last night, and by bedtime I felt nauseous. I had two loose stools. This morning I threw up and my blood sugar was 600 in the ambulance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had this before. Were you able to keep anything down after vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not really. I took Zofran but it didn’t help much. I got scared and called the ambulance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was the right call. Your blood sugar was very high—627 when you arrived—but you’re not in diabetic ketoacidosis, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not DKA? I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, your labs show no acidosis. We gave you IV insulin to bring it down. We also gave Zofran and Dilaudid for nausea and discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My stomach still feels off, but the pain is better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your exam shows no serious abdominal issues. Lungs are clear, heart normal. We did a chest X-ray to check for infection—it’s fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having a lot of back pain too, since my car accident years ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see you’re on gabapentin and Tylenol. We’ll continue those. No point tenderness in your back, so no new injury.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes… it’s always so hard to control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll talk more about that. For now, we’re starting you on fluids and will try to get you on a regular diet later today if you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’ve been doing well—no vomiting, and you kept down some crackers. We’re going to advance you to a regular diabetic diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I was worried I’d throw it up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor closely. Your blood sugar was high earlier after ice chips—did you know they have sugar in them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I didn’t! I thought it was just water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a common mistake. We’ll go over diet counseling to help avoid surprises like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood work came back. Your kidney function was a bit off when you arrived—creatinine 1.2—but it’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from my diabetes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it suggests early diabetic nephropathy. But staying hydrated and controlling your sugar helps protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know my kidneys were involved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s stage I, so very early. But it’s another reason to focus on tight glucose control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been trying… but my sugars swing so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed. You had a low sugar this morning—down to 60—after treating a high with too much insulin overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just wanted it to come down fast… I get so anxious when it’s high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. That’s actually something we want to talk about—your anxiety and how it affects your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes the nausea feels like it’s from panic, not my stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry saw you and thinks some episodes may be linked to anxiety ‘flooding,’ but this time, your symptoms may have been from food or high sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not all of it is in my head?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. We did a gastric emptying study yesterday—it was normal. So it’s not gastroparesis this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that test before and it was normal too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. So we’re focusing on diabetes control and possible gastroenteritis from the potato salad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back—no infection. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I didn’t have a blood infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Your symptoms weren’t from sepsis. We’re confident it’s related to your diabetes and possibly the food you ate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your A1C result—it’s 12.8%. That means your average sugar has been very high, around 321 mg/dL.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s worse than I thought.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We consulted diabetes management. They recommend keeping your Lantus at 28 units at night, but adjusting how you count carbs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought I was doing it right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You are trying, but we’re changing your ratio to 1 unit of Humalog for every 12 grams of carbs—was it 1:10 before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think so. And the sliding scale?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take 1 unit of Humalog for every 40 points your sugar is above 140. We’ll give you a chart to follow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s different. I’ll need to write it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and keep a log of your finger sticks. It’ll help your new doctor see patterns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve set up a lot for you before discharge tomorrow. You’ll see a new primary care provider in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve missed a lot of appointments before… I feel bad about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. That’s why a social worker will go with you to your first visit. They’ll help you connect with a therapist too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That would really help. I want to do better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. You also have a GI follow-up to repeat an endoscopy for your stomach varices and check if H. pylori is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well—no nausea, eating normally, sugars stable. We’re discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue Lantus 28 units at night, Humalog with meals using the new ratio. Gabapentin is now 200 mg three times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was 200 mg every 8 hours before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same total dose—just adjusted for easier timing. We’re also adding Zofran as a backup for nausea, but try Ativan first if anxiety is involved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pharmacy has your insulin and supplies. Keep checking your sugars and write them down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll go to the appointments—I promise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to support you. Call if your sugar is very high or low, or if vomiting returns. Otherwise, we’ll see how you do at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and good luck with your new care team.
